doc.title: Tim Ries interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 19, 2022

title: Sitting in around Detroit and Toledo, Soul Train, imitating Dad at the piano
summary: His father pushed him to saxophone, played swing and rock for parties, and drove him to sit in with Detroit and Toledo musicians. He loved Soul Train and improvised at the piano.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: one of his saxophone players so he was pushing me more towards hey, maybe — would you like to play the saxophone. So one day he brought a saxophone home like you know for a birthday or something like that. And I was quite young so I was starting to sit in with him when I was ten years old. So I was already curious about the music that he played, which was mostly older music like the swing era, like old jazz standards. But then he would also incorporate a couple of rock tunes, because younger people would want to play, you know “Proud Mary” or one of those rock-like, and he had to entertain the people. So I saw what it was like to play music and have to do different kinds of things, not just what you maybe liked but what the people might like. But then growing up in the Detroit area, when I was still too young to drive he would drive me to Detroit to sit in with musicians and then to Toledo, Ohio which was very close, and sitting in with like great jazz musicians. And there were so many of the Motown people that never left. When Motown moved to California they just stayed in Detroit and they were like fantastic jazz musicians. So I got to hear and play and sit in with all these great musicians. So I was always being introduced to great musicians and my dad would then have the musicians come back to our house and we would have jam sessions until five, six o’clock in the morning. And my mother would cook. So I was fall asleep on the couch to like this great music. And I remember as a kid like being, I don’t know like ten, eleven, twelve years old Saturday mornings watching “Soul Train.” Because that was like for me, I loved it. It was like listening to the greatest music ever. You know like I’m seeing the dancing and you know you’d see this little white kid who loved “Soul Train.” It was just like all music was good. You know it was like as if it was like essential. And I loved Stevie Wonder of course, Aretha, the Temptations, the Four Tops, and I got a chance then to play with all these people when I was older. So it was such a cool thing growing up. And so we had this big house with a lot of property, so I would go practice outside. So I had the advantage of being in a quiet like area, but then close enough to a bigger city to hang out with musicians and learn from them. So that was really amazing. So I was quite curious as a young person. And you know my dad played the trumpet but he would come home from his day job and sit at the piano, and he wasn’t trained as a pianist but then he would just kind of improvise and kind of compose this stuff. I remember being a little kid and I would be in there and I would watch him, not knowing what he was doing. And then he would leave and I would just sit at the piano and try to imitate that vibe. Because I think it was his way of just escaping the world, the workday, and that was his release. And I saw that in him. Like he was different on the piano than he was even on the trumpet, or just he was in this other world and I remember like that’s — he never said anything I just saw it. And it was like how do I capture that? And then my oldest sister, who was taking piano lessons, right, studying the piano — I wasn’t studying piano, I was © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

just trying to get that vibe. She came in, “What are you playing? That’s just nonsense” you know because I was just improvising. And because she said that it was like oh yeah well then I would do more.
